title: Queues vs Pub/Sub
summary: Point-to-point delivery vs fan-out — picked by who actually needs to receive the message, not by which broker looks fancier.

slides.markdown:
A message can go to exactly one consumer, or to every interested subscriber — picking the wrong pattern either duplicates work that should happen once, or misses reactions that should happen everywhere.

Queues implement point-to-point delivery: one message, one consumer, with multiple consumers competing for the same work. Pub/sub implements fan-out: one message, every subscriber gets its own copy. This topic is about deciding which shape a given message actually needs.

slides.sectionTitle: Point-to-point queues: one message, one consumer
slides.markdown:
A point-to-point queue delivers each message to exactly one consumer, even when several consumers are listening. Picture a queue of "resize this image" jobs: three worker processes pull from the same queue, but each job is picked up and processed by only one of them — never all three.

This is the right shape when the work must happen exactly once: charging a card, resizing an image, sending one email. If two workers processed the same "charge card" job, the customer gets billed twice.

The queue guarantees the message disappears (or is acknowledged) after one consumer successfully handles it — that's what makes "exactly one of my workers does this" possible.

Publish/subscribe flips the delivery model: every subscriber gets its own copy of the message, not just one of them. Publish an "order placed" event and the email service, the fraud-check service, and the analytics pipeline can all receive and process it independently.

This is the right shape when multiple, unrelated parts of the system each need to react to the same fact — nobody is competing for the work, because it isn't shared work, it's the same event mattering to several audiences.

Adding a new subscriber later, like a new analytics dashboard, doesn't require touching the publisher at all — it just starts listening.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: competing consumers vs pub/sub fan-out
slides.markdown:
![A queue splits messages across three competing worker consumers; a pub/sub topic clones one message into three separate subscriber queues](assets/competing-consumers-vs-fanout.svg)

In the competing-consumers picture, the messages split across workers — each message goes to exactly one of them. In the fan-out picture, the message is cloned — each subscriber's queue gets its own copy of the same message.

The visual difference is the tell in an interview: if your diagram shows work being *split*, you mean a queue; if it shows work being *copied*, you mean pub/sub.

slides.sectionTitle: Competing consumers pattern for horizontal scaling of workers
slides.markdown:
The **competing consumers** pattern is how a point-to-point queue scales horizontally: add more worker processes, all reading from the same queue, and the broker hands each message to whichever worker is free next.

This gets you load balancing for free — a burst of 500 jobs gets drained by however many workers are running, without any of them needing to know about the others. Add a fourth worker under load and it just starts picking up messages; no rebalancing logic to write.

The constraint: workers should be interchangeable and each message independent, since you can't control which worker gets which message.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: queue vs pub/sub — pick by "who should get this message"
slides.markdown:
| | Queue (point-to-point) | Pub/sub (fan-out) |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery | Exactly one consumer per message | Every subscriber gets a copy |
| Use when | The work should happen once | Multiple independent parties must react |
| Scaling model | Competing consumers share the load | Each subscriber scales its own consumption independently |
| Adding a new listener | Steals work from existing consumers | Adds a new, independent copy of the stream |

**How to decide:** ask "if I add a second listener, do I want it to share the existing work, or get its own full copy of every message?" Sharing means queue; full copy means pub/sub.

slides.sectionTitle: Topics and routing keys: filtering what a subscriber receives
slides.markdown:
Not every subscriber wants every message a publisher sends. **Topics** (or exchanges with routing keys) let a subscriber say "only send me messages tagged `orders.us`," instead of getting the full firehose and filtering client-side.

A payments team might subscribe to `orders.payment-failed` while a shipping team subscribes to `orders.confirmed` — both are subscribers to the same underlying stream of order events, but each only receives the slice that's relevant to it.

Routing keys turn pub/sub from "broadcast everything" into "broadcast selectively," which is what makes it viable once dozens of subscribers with different interests are involved.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: using pub/sub where you actually needed exactly one consumer to act
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Pub/sub is more flexible, so use it even for work that only one consumer should do."

**Why it's wrong:** if you publish a "charge this card" event to a topic with three subscribed payment workers, all three receive their own copy and all three charge the card — pub/sub has no notion of "only one of you should act on this."

**Correct model:** if exactly one consumer should perform an action, use a queue with competing consumers. Reach for pub/sub only when the message genuinely needs to reach multiple independent recipients.
